1: The U.S. is a republic: citizens elect people to represent them and make decisions for them.
2: The Constitution is the highest law. No other law, federal or state, can go against it.
3: The Constitution sets up the government, divides its powers, and protects people’s rights.
4: “We the People” means the power belongs to the people. The government gets its authority from them.
5: The Constitution changes through amendments. Remember: “amend” means to change.
6: The Bill of Rights is the first 10 amendments. It protects the basic rights of people in America.
7: The Constitution has 27 amendments. The first 10 are the Bill of Rights.
8: Adopted in 1776, it declared freedom from Britain and said all people are created equal.
9: The Declaration of Independence (1776) said the 13 colonies were free from British rule.
10: Both documents share big ideas like liberty and equality. Name any two from the list.
11: “Life, Liberty, and the pursuit of Happiness” comes from the Declaration of Independence, not the Constitution.
12: The U.S. has a capitalist, free market economy, where people and businesses own property and trade freely.
13: The rule of law means everyone, including leaders and the government, must obey the law. No one is above it.
14: The Declaration of Independence is the easiest answer to remember. The Articles of Confederation came right before the Constitution.
15: Three branches keep any one part from getting too powerful. Each branch checks the others.
16: Legislative (Congress) makes laws, executive (President) enforces them, and judicial (courts) explains them.
17: The President leads the executive branch, which carries out and enforces the laws.
18: Congress, the legislative branch, writes the laws.
19: Congress has two parts: the Senate and the House of Representatives.
20: Congress writes laws, declares war, and makes the federal budget. Name any one.
21: There are 100 U.S. senators: 2 for each of the 50 states.
22: Senators serve 6-year terms. There is no limit on how many terms they can serve.
23: Your answer depends on where you live. Find your two senators at senate.gov and save one in My State & Officials.
24: The House has 435 voting members, divided among the states by population.
25: Representatives serve 2-year terms, so the whole House is elected every 2 years.
26: Short 2-year terms keep representatives close to what voters want right now.
27: Every state has exactly 2 senators, whatever its size.
28: Equal Senate seats protect small states. This deal was called the Great Compromise.
29: Your answer depends on where you live. Find your representative at house.gov by entering your ZIP code.
30: The Speaker leads the House of Representatives. This name can change, so check uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates before your interview.
31: Each senator represents all the people of their state.
32: The citizens of each state vote to elect their senators.
33: A representative speaks for the people in their own congressional district.
34: The citizens who live in a congressional district elect its representative.
35: House seats are based on population, so states with more people get more representatives.
36: The President is elected every 4 years.
37: The 22nd Amendment limits the President to two terms, which keeps one person from holding power too long.
38: This name can change after an election. Check uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates before your interview.
39: This name can change after an election. Check uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates before your interview.
40: If the President dies, resigns, or cannot serve, the Vice President becomes President.
41: The President signs bills into law, vetoes bills, and commands the military. Name any one.
42: The President is Commander in Chief, which keeps the military under civilian control.
43: Congress passes a bill, then the President signs it to make it a law.
44: The President can veto (reject) a bill. Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote.
45: The President appoints (chooses) federal judges, and the Senate confirms them.
46: The executive branch includes the President, the Cabinet, and federal departments and agencies.
47: The Cabinet is a group of top officials who advise the President.
48: Easy picks: Vice-President and Attorney General, or Secretary of State. Name any two.
49: The Electoral College decides who is elected President. Each state’s electors cast the votes.
50: The Supreme Court is the best-known part of the judicial branch. The federal courts are also part of it.
51: The courts review and explain laws, settle disagreements, and decide if a law goes against the Constitution.
52: The Supreme Court is the highest court in the United States.
53: The Supreme Court has 9 seats: one Chief Justice and eight associate justices.
54: A majority of the 9 justices, which is 5, is usually needed to decide a case.
55: Supreme Court justices serve for life, or until they retire.
56: Life terms let justices decide cases fairly without worrying about politics or elections.
57: The Chief Justice leads the Supreme Court. Check uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates before your interview.
58: Only the federal government can print money, declare war, or make treaties with other countries.
59: States handle local needs like schools, police, and driver’s licenses.
60: The 10th Amendment says powers not given to the federal government belong to the states or to the people.
61: Your answer depends on where you live. Find your governor at usa.gov/states-and-territories.
62: Your answer depends on where you live. For example, the capital of California is Sacramento.
63: The voting amendments let citizens 18 and older vote, let women vote, ended poll taxes, and let men of any race vote. Describe one.
64: Only U.S. citizens can vote in federal elections, run for federal office, and serve on a jury.
65: Everyone living in the U.S., not just citizens, has these freedoms. Name any three.
66: The Pledge of Allegiance shows loyalty to the United States and its flag.
67: In the Oath of Allegiance, new citizens promise to obey U.S. laws and be loyal to the United States. Name any two promises.
68: You can become a citizen by being born here, by naturalizing (what you are doing now), or through your parents.
69: Voting and running for office are two easy examples of taking part in civic life.
70: Voting is the simplest answer. Paying taxes and serving in the military are also ways to serve.
71: Federal taxes are required by law and pay for the federal government.
72: Registering for Selective Service is required by law and keeps a draft fair if one is ever needed.
73: Many colonists came for freedom, including religious freedom and economic opportunity.
74: American Indians (Native Americans) lived here long before Europeans arrived.
75: People from Africa were taken and sold as slaves in America.
76: The Americans won independence in the American Revolution, also called the Revolutionary War.
77: “High taxes” or “taxation without representation” are the most common answers.
78: Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration of Independence.
79: The Declaration was adopted on July 4, 1776. That is why we celebrate the Fourth of July.
80: The Declaration of Independence itself counts as an important event of the Revolution.
81: Try this set: New York, New Jersey, New Hampshire, North Carolina, South Carolina. That’s three “New” states and the two Carolinas.
82: The U.S. Constitution was written in 1787 in Philadelphia.
83: James Madison, Alexander Hamilton, and John Jay wrote the Federalist Papers under the pen name “Publius.”
84: The Federalist Papers explained the Constitution and convinced people to support it.
85: Benjamin Franklin was an inventor, a U.S. diplomat, and helped write the Declaration of Independence.
86: George Washington was the first President, and he is called the “Father of Our Country.”
87: Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration of Independence and was the third President.
88: James Madison is the “Father of the Constitution” and was the fourth President.
89: Alexander Hamilton was the first Secretary of the Treasury and helped write the Federalist Papers.
90: In 1803, the Louisiana Purchase from France doubled the size of the United States.
91: The Civil War is the easiest answer. Others are the War of 1812 and the Mexican-American War.
92: The Civil War (1861–1865) was fought between the North and the South.
93: Easy answers: the Emancipation Proclamation, or “Lincoln was assassinated.”
94: Abraham Lincoln led the country during the Civil War, freed the slaves, and saved the Union.
95: Lincoln’s Emancipation Proclamation (1863) freed the slaves in the Confederate states.
96: The Civil War ended slavery in the United States.
97: The 14th Amendment makes people born or naturalized in the U.S. citizens.
98: After the Civil War, the 15th Amendment (1870) gave men of any race the right to vote.
99: Susan B. Anthony is the best-known leader of the women’s rights movement.
100: World War I, World War II, and the Korean, Vietnam, and Gulf Wars were all fought in the 1900s. Name any one.
101: The U.S. entered World War I because Germany attacked U.S. ships, and to support the Allied Powers.
102: Women won the right to vote in 1920 with the 19th Amendment, after World War I.
103: The Great Depression was the longest economic recession in modern history.
104: It started with the stock market crash of 1929, called the Great Crash.
105: Franklin Roosevelt (FDR) led the country through both the Great Depression and World War II.
106: The U.S. entered World War II after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in 1941.
107: Dwight Eisenhower was a general in World War II and later the 34th President.
108: The Soviet Union (USSR) was the main U.S. rival during the Cold War.
109: During the Cold War, the U.S. was concerned about communism and nuclear war.
110: The U.S. entered the Korean War to stop the spread of communism.
111: The U.S. entered the Vietnam War to stop the spread of communism, the same reason as the Korean War.
112: The civil rights movement fought to end racial discrimination.
113: Dr. King fought for civil rights and equality for all Americans.
114: The U.S. entered the Persian Gulf War to force the Iraqi military out of Kuwait.
115: On September 11, 2001, terrorists attacked the United States.
116: After 9/11, the U.S. fought the War in Afghanistan and the War in Iraq.
117: There are many tribes. Pick one that is easy to say, like Cherokee, Navajo, or Sioux.
118: The light bulb, the airplane, and landing on the moon are all American innovations.
119: Washington, D.C. is the capital of the United States.
120: The Statue of Liberty stands on Liberty Island in New York Harbor.
121: The 13 stripes stand for the 13 original colonies.
122: There are 50 stars, one for each state.
123: The national anthem is “The Star-Spangled Banner.”
124: “E Pluribus Unum” is Latin for “Out of many, one.”
125: Independence Day, July 4, celebrates U.S. independence from Britain. It is the country’s birthday.
126: An easy three to remember: New Year’s Day, Thanksgiving Day, and Christmas Day.
127: Memorial Day honors soldiers who died in military service.
128: Veterans Day honors everyone who has served in the U.S. military.
